draft.title: Research ethics
card: Research ethics are rules that protect the people who take part in an investigation. Participants are the people who provide the data.
Informed consent
a participant agrees to take part after being told what will happen and what the risks are. They can say no, or stop later, without a penalty.
Safety
the investigation must not put participants at risk of harm. A fitness test should suit their health and have supervision.
Privacy
personal information is kept private. Results are stored securely and shared in a way that does not name the person.
draft.remember: Ethical research asks first, keeps people safe and keeps their information private.

a.q: Which action shows that a group has gained informed consent from a classmate?
opts: They explain the test and risks, then the classmate agrees
They give the classmate the test time and expect them to come
They let the classmate join in only if the class votes yes
They start the test and ask the classmate to say if it hurts
a.why: Informed consent means the person is told what will happen and the risks, and then agrees. Starting the test first is wrong because the classmate has not yet agreed with full information.
a.clue: The person must know the details before they agree.

b.q: Priya's group runs a survey on sleep habits in Year 9. She wants to post each student's name and answers on the school noticeboard. Which ethical principle would this break?
opts: Privacy, as answers could be linked to named students
Safety, as students might be hurt reading the noticeboard
Consent, as students were not told the survey's purpose
Safety, as sleep surveys carry a risk of physical harm
b.why: Showing names beside answers means personal information is not kept private. Consent is the tempting choice, but nothing in the case says the students were not told about the survey. The problem is how the results are shared.
b.clue: Look at what happens to the answers after they are collected.

problems.detail: The Safety line says the investigation 'must not put participants at risk of harm', but the consent line says participants are told 'what the risks are'. These clash, and any fitness test carries some risk. Ethical research reduces risk and manages it; it cannot remove all risk. Better: 'the investigation should keep the risk of harm as low as possible'.
